analysis.one_liner: Sets EPA deadlines to write water pollution limits for PFAS "forever chemicals" discharged by factories.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced with four sponsors from both parties and 22 cosponsors, it died without a markup or a vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS are long-lasting industrial chemicals linked to health problems that have contaminated water across the country. This bill would order the EPA to write national water quality criteria for PFAS within three years and to set discharge limits for specific industries — chemical and plastics makers, electroplaters, textile mills, landfills, tanneries, paint and plastics plants — on a phased schedule. It would also require monitoring of discharges starting immediately, standardize the EPA's PFAS testing method, and send $1 billion over five years in grants to municipal wastewater plants to keep PFAS out of waterways.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who drink water, swim in, or fish from rivers contaminated by industrial PFAS discharges; communities near PFAS-emitting plants; and municipal wastewater utilities, which get federal grants to handle PFAS coming into their plants.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the EPA to publish human health water quality criteria for every measurable PFAS substance within three years of enactment.

Sets firm deadlines — June 2025, 2026, and 2027 — for the EPA to finalize discharge limits for chemical and plastics makers, electroplating and metal finishing, textile mills, landfills, leather tanning, paint formulating, and plastics molding plants, covering discharges sent to public treatment works too.
Requires monitoring of PFAS discharges in those industries starting on the day of enactment, plus monitoring for pulp and paper mills, airports, and electrical component manufacturers.
Orders the EPA to formally adopt its validated PFAS test method (Method 1633) by January 2025, which makes enforceable measurement possible.
Authorizes $200 million per year for fiscal 2024–2028 in grants to publicly owned treatment works for PFAS pretreatment and source monitoring, easing the burden on local utilities and ratepayers.

analysis.who_pays: Industries that discharge PFAS into water — chemical manufacturers, electroplaters, textile mills, tanneries, and similar plants — would bear the cost of monitoring, pretreatment, and cutting PFAS out of their wastewater; some costs could reach consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on discharging plants, including smaller textile, tanning, and metal-finishing shops; some of that cost can be passed to consumers through higher prices.
The grant program is only authorized, not guaranteed — it is funded 'subject to the availability of appropriations,' so utilities could face new monitoring duties without the promised federal money.
The bill only covers PFAS that can be measured with an EPA-approved test method, leaving unmeasurable substances outside the limits.
It regulates ongoing discharges but does nothing to clean up PFAS already in soil, sediment, and groundwater from past pollution.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong: PFAS do not break down and exposure is linked to serious health harms, so stopping industrial discharges at the source protects drinking water for millions. The main honest cost is compliance spending by discharging industries, some of which passes to consumers; the bill tries to soften the burden on local utilities with grants, but those grants depend on future appropriations. On balance, the public health gain outweighs the compliance cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee in April 2024, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Pappas introduced the bill on April 18, 2024, joined by Reps. Brian Fitzpatrick, Dan Kildee, and Bill Posey — two Democrats and two Republicans.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup and the House never voted on the bill before the 118th Congress ended.
The bill had 22 cosponsors, 19 Democrats and 3 Republicans, when the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS-discharging industries are better off: they face no federal discharge limits for these chemicals, and the public keeps bearing the health and cleanup costs.

for.name: Chris Pappas
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to set PFAS discharge limits and water quality criteria.

against.name: Sam Graves
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee never took up the bill; no markup or floor action occurred before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: the four original sponsors split two Democrats and two Republicans, and final cosponsors were 19 Democrats and 3 Republicans.

industries.industry: Chemical, plastics, and synthetic fiber manufacturers
industries.note: First in line for enforceable PFAS discharge limits by mid-2025; their interest in avoiding treatment costs runs against the public's interest in clean drinking water.
Facing the same 2025 deadline for PFAS discharge limits and monitoring; resisting limits means communities keep absorbing the contamination.

industries.industry: Textile mills, landfills, tanneries, and paint and plastics formulators
industries.note: Phased limits in 2026 and 2027 for these dischargers, including flows sent to public treatment plants.

industries.industry: Pulp and paper mills, airports, and electrical component makers
industries.note: Required to monitor PFAS discharges immediately, but limits depend on a later EPA determination, so the near-term cost is testing rather than treatment.
Would receive $200 million a year in grants for PFAS pretreatment and source tracking, taking cost off local ratepayers while the discharge limits upstream reduce the PFAS reaching their plants.
